sections.title: What Is Cocaine?
body: Cocaine is a popular stimulant used across the globe. The National Institute on Drug Abuse reported that approximately 5.2 million individuals in the United States reported using cocaine during the year of 2020 . An estimated 1.3 million of the individuals who used cocaine in 2020 were living with a cocaine use disorder.

Cocaine is commonly cut with other white powders, which can include powerful opioids such as fentanyl. This increases a person’s risk of overdosing. In 2020, there were 19,447 individuals who had a fatal overdose involving cocaine.

sections.title: How Does Cocaine Affect the Body?
body: The way that cocaine is used contributes to some of the differences you may see in how your body is impacted by your cocaine use. As an example, someone who uses cocaine intravenously may have more bruising, collapsed veins, or transmitted infections and diseases. Smoking can cause damage to an individual’s mouth, whereas snorting is known to damage a person’s nasal cavity.

Regardless of how a person uses cocaine, the impact on their brains will be similar. Once cocaine is ingested, our brains are told to release more dopamine. Dopamine is a naturally occurring chemical in our brain that contributes to feelings of pleasure and euphoria. The increase of dopamine after using cocaine leads to feelings of euphoria which can increase a person’s desire to continue cocaine use. As a person’s use of cocaine continues, the amount of dopamine released increases.

Your brain will continue to release a surge of dopamine when you first stop using, and needs time with you not using to recognize that it needs to decrease the amount of dopamine it releases. This shift is a contributing factor to the presence of withdrawal symptoms when you stop using. Detox programs will monitor your withdrawal symptoms and work with you to provide relief where possible.
